title: Do not force broken literal sequence (Philoc. 8)
english: Where the letter’s sequence is solecistic or will not cohere, do not torture the text into a wooden narrative; seek the sense the Spirit intends without pretending every hitch is history.
translator_notes: Copy-text Robinson 1893 Philocalia TEI (origen_tlg019.xml); no George Lewis 1911 wording.

title: Same name, different senses (Philoc. 9)
english: Scripture often uses one name for many things; the same word may be virtue here and vice there. The reader must test the [[sense of the words >> Bible:Nehemiah 8:8]] by context and the analogy of the faith.

title: Stumbling-stone passages (Philoc. 10)
english: Things in Scripture that seem a [[stone of stumbling >> Bible:Isaiah 8:14]] are there so that the lazy do not claim to have understood everything, and the diligent dig for the Spirit’s meaning.

title: Hard texts that heal (Philoc. 11)
english: Passages that look harsh or strange are medicines; they wound pride and heal the soul that will stay with the Word.

title: When philosophy helps (Philoc. 13)
english: Philosophy can serve the interpretation of the sacred writings when it is a handmaid, not a mistress — taken selectively, under the rule of faith, not as a rival gospel.
